title: jq
description: jq — a lightweight and flexible command-line JSON processor, sometimes described as 'sed for JSON.' Filters, transforms, slices, maps, and reshapes JSON with a small functional query language.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`jq` is a single self-contained binary. It reads JSON from stdin (or a
file argument) and writes transformed JSON (or other text) to stdout.

## Current version and project home

The latest stable release is **jq 1.8.2** (June 2026). Note that the
project is now maintained at
[github.com/jqlang/jq](https://github.com/jqlang/jq) — the original
`stedolan/jq` repository went dormant after 1.6/1.7 and the community fork
under the `jqlang` organization is the actively maintained project today.
If you find older tutorials linking to `stedolan/jq`, the content is
still largely accurate, but file issues and check releases against
`jqlang/jq` instead.

## Install on Arch Linux

```bash
sudo pacman -S jq
```

## Install elsewhere

```bash
# macOS
brew install jq

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install jq
```

## Check your version

```bash
jq --version
```

## Your first filter

```bash
echo '{"name": "reqly", "version": "0.3.0"}' | jq '.name'
```

Output:

```
"reqly"
```

`.` is the identity filter (return the input unchanged); `.name` accesses
the `name` field. jq pretty-prints by default with 2-space indentation and
colorized output when writing to a terminal.

```bash
cat pubspec.yaml.json | jq '.dependencies'
curl -s https://api.example.com/data | jq '.results[0]'
```

See [Core Concepts](/jq/core-concepts/) for how filters, the pipe
operator, and the object/array construction syntax fit together.
Getting Started.Core Concepts:
## Filters and the pipe operator

Every jq program is a **filter**: something that takes JSON in and
produces JSON out. Filters compose with `|`, much like shell pipes, but
operating on JSON values rather than text streams:

```bash
jq '.users | .[0] | .name'
```

is equivalent to the more idiomatic:

```bash
jq '.users[0].name'
```

## Identity, field access, and indexing

```bash
.                 # identity: return input unchanged
.foo              # field "foo" of an object
.foo.bar          # nested field access
.foo?             # like .foo but doesn't error if input isn't an object
.[0]              # first element of an array
.[2:5]            # array slice, indices 2 up to (not including) 5
.[]               # iterate: emit every element of an array or every value of an object
```

## Multiple outputs, not a single return value

A jq filter can produce **zero, one, or many** outputs for a single
input — this is the single most important conceptual difference from most
languages. `.[]` on an array of 5 elements emits 5 separate JSON values,
one per line by default:

```bash
echo '[1,2,3]' | jq '.[]'
```

```
1
2
3
```

This is what makes jq's pipe-based composition so powerful: each stage
can fan a single input out into many, or collapse many back into one
(e.g. with `add`, `length`, or wrapping in `[...]`).

## Exit status

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Success, and (with `-e`) the last output was not `false`/`null`. |
| `1` | Filter compile error or runtime error. |
| `4` | (with `-e`) success but last output was `false` or `null`. |

`-e`/`--exit-status` is the flag to reach for when using jq in scripts as
a boolean check:

```bash
if jq -e '.enabled' config.json > /dev/null; then
  echo "enabled"
fi
```

## Raw vs JSON-encoded output

```bash
jq '.name'           # "reqly"   <- JSON-encoded string, with quotes
jq -r '.name'         # reqly     <- raw string, no quotes
```

`-r`/`--raw-output` is essential any time you want to feed jq's output
into a shell variable or another command without JSON string quoting
getting in the way.

See [Filters & Syntax](/jq/filters-and-syntax/) for the rest of the query
language and [Building & Transforming](/jq/building-and-transforming/) for
constructing new JSON shapes.

Guides.Filters & Syntax:
## Object and array construction

```bash
jq '{name: .name, ver: .version}'         # build a new object
jq '[.name, .version]'                    # build a new array
jq '{(.key): .value}'                     # computed key name
```

## Pipe, comma, and parentheses

```bash
jq '.a, .b'          # comma: emit BOTH .a and .b as separate outputs
jq '.a | .b'          # pipe: feed .a's output into .b
jq '(.a, .b) | length'  # parens control precedence, like in math
```

## Optional access with `?`

```bash
jq '.foo?'                # suppress error if input has no .foo / isn't an object
jq '.items[]?'             # suppress error if .items is missing or not iterable
```

## Select, map, and filtering arrays

```bash
jq '.[] | select(.active == true)'
jq 'map(select(.price > 10))'
jq 'map(.name)'
```

`select(cond)` is the core filtering primitive: it emits its input
unchanged if `cond` is truthy, and emits nothing otherwise — combined with
`.[]` or `map()`, this is how jq expresses "keep only the items matching
X."

## Built-in functions (a practical subset)

| Function | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `length` | Length of a string, array, or object. |
| `keys` | Sorted array of an object's keys. |
| `values` | Array of an object's values. |
| `has("k")` | Whether an object has key `"k"`. |
| `contains(x)` | Whether the input contains `x` (substring/subset). |
| `type` | `"object"`, `"array"`, `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"null"`. |
| `add` | Sum a numeric array, or concatenate a string/array array. |
| `sort`, `sort_by(f)` | Sort an array, optionally by a key function. |
| `unique`, `unique_by(f)` | Deduplicate. |
| `group_by(f)` | Group array elements into sub-arrays by key. |
| `min_by(f)` / `max_by(f)` | Element with min/max key value. |
| `to_entries` / `from_entries` | Object ↔ array of `{key, value}` pairs. |
| `flatten` | Flatten nested arrays. |
| `reverse` | Reverse an array or string. |
| `empty` | Produce no output at all (useful inside `select`/`if`). |

## String interpolation and `@` format filters

```bash
jq -r '"\(.name) v\(.version)"'      # string interpolation
jq -r '.name | @base64'                # encode as base64
jq -r '.csv_row | @csv'                 # format an array as CSV
jq -r '.url_part | @uri'                # URL-encode
```

## Conditionals

```bash
jq 'if .active then "on" else "off" end'
jq 'if .score >= 90 then "A" elif .score >= 80 then "B" else "F" end'
```

## Regex support (added in jq 1.5, still current)

```bash
jq -r '.email | test("^[^@]+@[^@]+$")'         # boolean
jq -r '.text | capture("(?<user>\\w+)@(?<host>.+)")'
jq -r '.text | [scan("\\d+")]'                 # all number-like substrings
jq -r '.text | sub("foo"; "bar")'                # first-match replace
jq -r '.text | gsub("foo"; "bar")'               # global replace
```

See [Building & Transforming](/jq/building-and-transforming/) for
reshaping data end to end, and [CLI Options](/jq/cli-options/) for the
flag reference.
Guides.Building & Transforming:
## Reshaping an array of objects

```bash
echo '[{"id":1,"name":"a"},{"id":2,"name":"b"}]' | jq 'map({(.name): .id})'
```

## Grouping and aggregating

```bash
jq 'group_by(.category) | map({category: .[0].category, count: length})'
```

```bash
jq 'group_by(.category) | map({(.[0].category): (map(.amount) | add)}) | add'
```

## Flattening nested structures

```bash
jq '[.. | numbers]'          # recursively find every number anywhere in the input
jq '[paths]'                  # every path in the document, as arrays
jq 'getpath(["a","b","c"])'   # access a deeply nested value by path array
```

`..` is the recursive descent operator — it emits the input and every
value reachable from it at any depth, which combined with a type filter
(`numbers`, `strings`, `objects`, `arrays`) is a common way to pull out
every value of a given kind anywhere in a document.

## Merging objects

```bash
jq -s '.[0] * .[1]' a.json b.json    # deep merge two JSON files
```

`-s`/`--slurp` reads all inputs into a single array first, which is what
makes `.[0] * .[1]` possible when merging two separate files. `*` on two
objects performs a recursive merge (right side wins on conflicts).

## Updating values in place with `|=`, `+=`

```bash
jq '.count += 1'
jq '.items[] |= (.price *= 1.1)'
jq 'del(.debug)'                       # remove a key
jq '.config.env = "production"'         # set/overwrite a field
```

`|=` updates a value using a filter that receives the *old* value as
input — this is the idiomatic way to modify JSON in place rather than
rebuilding the whole structure.

## Converting between JSON and other formats

```bash
jq -r '.[] | [.name, .price] | @csv'    # JSON array -> CSV rows
jq -R -s 'split("\n")'                  # raw lines -> JSON array of strings
jq -c '.'                                # compact (single-line) output
```

`-R`/`--raw-input` treats each input line as a raw string rather than
parsing it as JSON — essential when converting plain text into JSON, or
combined with `-s`/`--slurp` to read the whole input as one big string
first.

## In-place file editing pattern

jq never edits files in place directly. The idiomatic pattern is:

```bash
jq '.version = "1.1.0"' pubspec.json > tmp.json && mv tmp.json pubspec.json
```

(`sponge` from moreutils, or newer jq's undocumented behavior of writing
to a temp file via shell redirection tricks, are common alternatives — but
the temp-file-and-mv pattern above is the most portable and safe one.)

See [CLI Options](/jq/cli-options/) for the flags used across these
examples and [Recipes](/jq/recipes/) for full worked scripts.
Guides.CLI Options:
## Output formatting

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-r` / `--raw-output` | Print strings without JSON quoting. |
| `-c` / `--compact-output` | One JSON value per line, no pretty-printing. |
| `-j` / `--join-output` | Like `-r` but without a trailing newline after each output. |
| `-a` / `--ascii-output` | Escape all non-ASCII characters. |
| `-S` / `--sort-keys` | Sort object keys alphabetically in output. |
| `-C` / `--color-output` | Force color even when not a terminal. |
| `-M` / `--monochrome-output` | Disable color even in a terminal. |
| `--tab` | Indent with tabs instead of 2 spaces. |
| `--indent N` | Use N spaces of indentation. |

## Input handling

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-n` / `--null-input` | Don't read any input; useful for pure computation or generating JSON from scratch. |
| `-R` / `--raw-input` | Treat each input line as a raw string, not JSON. |
| `-s` / `--slurp` | Read all inputs into a single JSON array before filtering. |
| `-e` / `--exit-status` | Set exit code based on the last output's truthiness. |

```bash
jq -n '{generated: now, host: "localhost"}'   # build JSON from nothing
```

## Passing external values into a filter

```bash
jq --arg name "reqly" '.project = $name'                  # $name is a string
jq --argjson threshold 10 'select(.count > $threshold)'    # $threshold is parsed as JSON
jq --slurpfile extra other.json '.extra = $extra'           # $extra is other.json's full content
```

`--arg` always injects a string; `--argjson` parses the value as JSON
first (so numbers/booleans/objects come through as their real type, not a
string).

## Modules and custom functions (jq 1.5+)

```jq
def double: . * 2;
map(double)
```

Custom functions can be defined inline in a filter, or in a `.jq` file
imported with `import`/`include` for reuse across scripts — useful once a
filter grows past a one-liner.

## Error handling

```bash
jq '.foo // "default"'                 # // is the "alternative" operator: fallback if .foo is null/false
jq 'try .foo catch "error!"'            # catch runtime errors from a filter
jq '.foo? // empty'                     # suppress AND fall through with no output
```

See [Recipes](/jq/recipes/) for these assembled into full command-line
workflows.
Guides.Recipes:
## Pretty-print a JSON file

```bash
jq '.' data.json
```

## Extract a single value for use in a shell script

```bash
VERSION=$(jq -r '.version' pubspec.json)
echo "Building version $VERSION"
```

## Filter an array of objects by a field

```bash
jq '.packages[] | select(.name | startswith("dart_"))' deps.json
```

## Sum a numeric field across an array

```bash
jq '[.orders[].total] | add' orders.json
```

## Count items matching a condition

```bash
jq '[.[] | select(.status == "failed")] | length' results.json
```

## Convert an API response into CSV

```bash
curl -s https://api.example.com/users \
  | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .name, .email] | @csv'
```

## Merge two config files (later file wins on conflicts)

```bash
jq -s '.[0] * .[1]' base.json overrides.json > merged.json
```

## Turn a newline-separated list into a JSON array

```bash
cat names.txt | jq -R -s -c 'split("\n") | map(select(length > 0))'
```

## Bump a version field in place

```bash
jq '.version = "1.2.0"' pubspec.json > tmp.$$ && mv tmp.$$ pubspec.json
```

## Pull nested error messages out of a GitHub Actions-style JSON log

```bash
jq -r '.. | objects | select(has("level") and .level == "error") | .message' ci.log.json
```

## Watch a JSON API and alert on a threshold

```bash
if jq -e '.queue_depth > 100' status.json > /dev/null; then
  echo "ALERT: queue backing up"
fi
```

## Use jq as a lightweight JSON validator

```bash
jq empty file.json && echo "valid JSON" || echo "invalid JSON"
```

`empty` produces no output at all; combined with jq's own parse step,
this checks validity without printing anything on success.

Project.FAQ:
### Is `jq` still maintained? I see old links to stedolan/jq.

Yes. Development moved to
[jqlang/jq](https://github.com/jqlang/jq) after the original maintainer
(Stephen Dolan, `stedolan`) became less active. The current stable release
under that project is **1.8.2** (June 2026). Older tutorials linking to
`stedolan/jq` are generally still accurate for syntax, but check the
`jqlang` org for current releases, issues, and documentation.

### Why does my filter print more than one value?

jq filters can emit zero, one, or many outputs per input — this is normal,
not an error. `.[]` in particular fans an array or object out into one
output per element. Wrap the result in `[...]` to collapse it back into a
single array if that's what you want.

### How do I get plain text out instead of quoted JSON strings?

Use `-r`/`--raw-output`. Without it, `jq '.name'` prints `"reqly"` (with
quotes, since it's JSON-encoded); with `-r` it prints `reqly`.

### Does jq edit files in place?

No, not directly. The standard pattern is to redirect to a temp file and
then move it over the original:

```bash
jq '.field = "value"' file.json > tmp.json && mv tmp.json file.json
```

### What's the difference between `.foo` and `.foo?`

`.foo` raises an error if the input isn't an object (e.g. it's `null` or
an array). `.foo?` suppresses that error and simply produces no output
instead — useful when iterating over a mixed collection where not every
item has the field.

### How do I pass a shell variable into a jq filter?

Use `--arg name value` (injects as a JSON string) or `--argjson name value`
(parses `value` as JSON first, preserving its real type):

```bash
jq --arg env "$ENVIRONMENT" '.env = $env' config.json
```

### Where do I report bugs or read the changelog?

The project lives at
[github.com/jqlang/jq](https://github.com/jqlang/jq). Release notes are
published per version on the GitHub releases page there, and the manual
is mirrored at [jqlang.org](https://jqlang.org).
